name: AI Action Review Pattern
description: A framework-agnostic pattern for reviewing AI-proposed actions before they run: plan preview, affected data, risk labels, scoped permissions, approve, reject, and edit controls, undo, progress, partial failure handling, and an audit trail. It defines the control surface for actions with consequences, and composes with the AI Agent Chat Layout and the AI Response Rendering Pattern.

aiAgentInstructions.summary: Build a review surface for actions an AI agent proposes, as a state machine over one or more proposed actions. Show what the agent plans to do and why, what it affects, which permission it uses, whether it can be undone, and how risky it is. Let people approve, approve selected actions, reject, edit, ask for a revised plan, pause or stop, retry failures, undo, and read the audit trail. Build on the project's dialog, drawer, button, checkbox, disclosure, and table components, and its permission and audit services. Implement only what the task needs, keep existing APIs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults; if one conflicts with an accessibility, security, or correctness requirement in this guide, ask the user instead of choosing silently. Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
keyFeatures: A structured action model with stable ids, the action type, affected objects, permission scope, destination, inputs, risk level, reversibility, state, idempotency key, and audit details
A plain-language plan summary first, then details behind disclosures: raw payloads, policy checks, and the evidence behind the proposal
Risk levels low, medium, high, and blocked, shown with text and an icon, never color alone
Review controls: Approve (named for the action), Approve selected, Reject, Edit, and Ask for revision
Execution controls: Pause, Stop, Retry, Undo, and View log

Confirmation that scales with consequence: one approval for low risk, an explicit review step for high risk, a typed confirmation (paste allowed) for actions that can't be undone, and no approval for blocked actions
Lifecycle states: proposed, reviewing, needs-changes, approved, executing, paused, completed, partially-completed, failed, cancelled, reverted
Partial failures keep every action's result visible, and a retry never runs an action twice
Task-scoped permission requests instead of broad, lasting grants
An audit trail with the action, actor, approver, time, tool, inputs, outputs, outcome, and rollback
Inline, side-panel, drawer, or modal review; a modal review follows the Dialog guide
implementationSteps: 1. Detect the framework and its version, the styling system, the tokens, and the existing components (projectDetection), plus the project's dialog, drawer, and table components, its permission and audit services, and any chat or response-rendering code it already has. Build on them, and keep their APIs.
2. Choose what the task needs: the review surfaces, partial approval, editing, pause, undo, and the audit trail. Leave out the rest.
3. Map the agent's proposals to typed action items (dataStructures.actionItem). An unknown action type still renders as a reviewable item and is never approved automatically.
4. Implement the review lifecycle and the item states (stateManagement).
5. Render the review: the header, the plan summary before any details, the action list, and the details disclosures (implementationDetails).
6. Apply the confirmation rules by risk (implementationDetails.confirmationRules, frameworkPatterns.typedConfirmation).

7. Wire editing with the project's form validation, and the execution controls: Pause, Stop, Retry, Undo, and View log. Give each approved action an idempotency key that retries reuse (frameworkPatterns.idempotentRetry).
8. Record the audit events, and request only task-scoped permissions.
9. Add the accessibility behavior in patternSpec.accessibility and the layouts in responsiveBreakpoints.
10. Check the result against testingChecklist with a keyboard, a screen reader, and a phone, and run the project's existing tests and checks.

patternSpec.problem: AI agents draft emails, update records, run tools, create files, schedule meetings, and call APIs. If actions with consequences run without a clear review step, people may not know what the agent plans to do, which data or people are affected, whether it can be undone, what permission it uses, how to correct the plan, how to interrupt it, or what happened afterward. A plain confirmation dialog is too vague and too binary for agent workflows that need editing, partial approval, scoped permissions, undo, and an audit trail.
patternSpec.solution: Treat the review as a state machine over one or more proposed actions. Turn the proposal into typed actions, summarize the goal in plain language, and show what each action affects, where it goes, which permission it uses, when it happens, and whether it can be undone. Label risk with text and an icon, and scale the confirmation to it. Give controls to approve, approve selected actions, reject, edit, ask for a revision, pause, stop, retry, undo, and read the log. Keep partial results, never run an action twice, and record an audit trail. Build on the project's own chat, dialog, table, form, and button conventions.
do: Show proposed actions before anything runs, built from a structured action model with stable ids, never from generated prose alone

Summarize the goal in plain language before technical payloads, and say what led to the proposal; when it follows outside content, such as an email, a web page, or a shared file, say so, since instructions in it may not come from the user
Show affected objects, destination, permission scope, data sources, and reversibility
Label risk as low, medium, high, or blocked with text and an icon, not color alone
Name Approve for the action and its scope, such as "Send to 3 recipients" or "Update 43 records"
Let people approve, approve selected actions, reject, edit, or ask the assistant for a revised plan
Require a stronger confirmation for high-risk and irreversible actions, and block approval when permissions are missing, parameters are invalid, or a policy check fails, saying what must change
Keep Pause, Stop, Retry, Undo, and View log reachable during and after execution when they apply
Give each approved action an idempotency key and reuse it on every retry, and treat no answer (a timeout or a dropped connection) as an unknown outcome
Keep partial results in place, with completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, and reverted actions told apart
Request the narrowest permission that can complete the task, and record audit events
Check permission and approval again on the server; the review surface is not the security boundary
dont: Run actions with consequences straight from an assistant message without review
Hide recipients, affected records, file paths, destinations, or permissions behind generic text
Give a high-risk action the same one-click approval as a low-risk draft
Use vague confirmation copy, such as "Are you sure?", without concrete consequences
Force all-or-nothing approval when independent actions can be selected safely
Replace partial results with a generic error, or retry an action in a way that can run it twice
Grant broad or lasting permissions when task-scoped access is enough
Use hold-to-confirm, or block paste in a typed confirmation
examples: Sending an email: show the recipients, subject, body, attachments, the context it came from, and when it sends, and flag external recipients. People can edit the text, remove recipients, save it as a draft, approve, or ask for a softer tone.
A bulk record update: 43 proposed customer updates grouped by risk, with a sample diff and selectable rows. People approve the low-risk changes and reject one high-risk change.

Scheduling: show attendees, time zone, conflicts, conferencing, external guests, the agenda, and whether personal calendar access is used. People can change the time or the attendees before approving.

Sharing a file: show the file, its current access, the proposed recipients, the access level, any expiry, inherited permissions, and whether the share can be revoked. A public link needs explicit confirmation.
A code change: show the touched files, the diff, the commands the agent wants to run, the permission to run them, the test plan, and how to roll back. Commands run only after approval.
A payment or an order: show the amount, account, recipient, invoice, due date, fees, and whether it can be cancelled, with high-risk confirmation and audit logging.
A permission request: show the exact missing scope, why this action needs it, for how long, and a manual alternative when there is one.

A partial failure: five actions were approved. Three completed, one failed validation, and one was skipped because it depended on the failed one. The review stays visible, with Retry for the failure and Undo for the completed actions.

No answer: the request to send an invoice times out, or its connection drops. The action says it's unknown whether the invoice was sent, and Retry reuses its idempotency key, so the server sends it at most once.

requirements.1.3.1: Action groups, details, labels, status, and errors are programmatically associated.
requirements.1.4.1: Risk and status are never shown by color alone.
requirements.1.4.3: Text and status labels have at least 4.5:1 contrast.
requirements.1.4.11: Focus indicators, controls, icons, borders, and risk indicators have at least 3:1 contrast.
requirements.2.1.1: Every review, selection, disclosure, approval, and execution control works from the keyboard.
requirements.2.4.3: Focus follows the review task, and progress updates never move it.
requirements.2.4.7: Every control shows a visible focus indicator.
requirements.2.4.11: Sticky controls never cover the focused element: scroll-padding matches their height.
requirements.2.5.8: Controls are at least 24 by 24 CSS px, or have enough space around them.
requirements.3.2.2: Selecting an action or editing a parameter never runs anything.
requirements.3.3.1: Blocked, invalid, failed, unknown, and failed-rollback states are described in text.
requirements.3.3.3: Validation and permission failures say how to proceed.
requirements.3.3.4: Actions with consequences can be reviewed, confirmed, corrected, or cancelled before they run.
requirements.4.1.2: Buttons, checkboxes, disclosures, and modal surfaces expose their roles and states.
requirements.4.1.3: Lifecycle updates are announced without moving focus.

keyboardNavigation.description: The whole review works from the keyboard, and nothing runs by surprise.
requirements: Tab reaches every control, action checkbox, details disclosure, and execution control, in the order of the task
Space toggles an action's selection and a disclosure; Enter activates the focused button
Escape closes a modal review as Cancel and never approves; in a high-risk confirmation step it cancels the step and returns to the review

screenReaderSupport.description: Screen reader users understand the proposal, the risk, the selection, the progress, and the outcome.
requirements: Headings for the review title, the plan summary, the action list, and the audit trail
Each selectable action's name contains its title and consequence; its risk label is text
aria-describedby connects each action to its consequence, permission, and reversibility

Lifecycle updates, such as executing, completed, failed, cancelled, and reverted, go through one polite status region: the conversation's when the review sits in a chat, its own otherwise. A modal review makes everything outside it inert, which hides the conversation's region, so while it's open it announces through a status region inside the dialog
role="alert" only for urgent failures that need attention now
Progress logs are never streamed into a live region

focusManagement.description: Focus supports review and correction without surprise jumps.
requirements: A modal review follows the Dialog guide: native <dialog> opened with showModal(), or the rest of the page inert, with focus on the heading or the first safe control, and back on the invoking control when it closes
An inline, side-panel, or drawer review moves focus to its heading when it opens
High-risk confirmations put focus on the least destructive action
A validation failure moves focus to the first invalid field; a permission failure to the explanation or the scoped request
After Undo, focus stays near the affected action, and the result is announced

actionItem.description: An action item. Adapt the field names to the project, and keep their meaning.

fields.name: id
fields.notes: Stable; never key rows by index

fields.name: actionType
fields.notes: message, record-update, file-operation, schedule, code-change, payment-or-order, external-api, system-setting, unknown

fields.name: affectedObjects
fields.notes: Records, files, people, recipients, settings, invoices, orders, or other things it changes

fields.name: permissions
fields.notes: The scopes it needs, or already has

fields.name: inputs
fields.notes: Parameters people can edit or inspect

fields.name: destination
fields.notes: An external system, recipient, repository, account, or integration

fields.name: source
fields.notes: What led to the proposal, such as the message or the email, page, or file it came from

fields.name: state
fields.notes: proposed, selected, blocked, approved, executing, completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, reverted

fields.name: failure
fields.notes: Why a failed action failed: error, when the app reported a failure, or outcome-unknown, when no answer came (a timeout or a dropped connection) or a gateway answered instead of the app

fields.name: idempotencyKey
fields.notes: Created when the action is approved and reused on every retry, so the server runs it at most once

fields.name: auditMetadata
fields.notes: Actor, approver, time, tool, integration, policy checks, an input hash, an output reference, and a rollback id

riskLevels.low: Reversible, local, expected, limited in scope
riskLevels.medium: Changes shared data, several targets, or saved state
riskLevels.high: External, sensitive, costly, changes permissions, destructive, or hard to undo
riskLevels.blocked: Invalid, missing a permission, failing a policy check, unsupported, or missing a prerequisite

reversibility.reversible: The system can undo it, or restore the previous state
reversibility.partially-reversible: Some of it can be undone, but side effects may remain
reversibility.irreversible: It can't be undone once it runs
reversibility.unknown: The system can't guarantee a rollback; treat it as higher risk

states.purpose: The agent's proposal is ready, and nobody has reviewed it
Someone is reading, selecting, or editing actions
Someone edited inputs or asked for a revised plan
The selected actions are approved, and none has started
Some actions completed, and others failed, were skipped, or were cancelled
Someone stopped the run before it finished

transitions: proposed to reviewing when the review opens
reviewing to needs-changes on an edit or a request for revision, and back to proposed when the agent sends a revised plan
reviewing to approved when someone approves eligible selected actions, and approved to executing when they start
executing to paused and back, when someone pauses and resumes a run of several steps
executing to completed, partially-completed, failed, or cancelled (Stop starts no new action; one already sent may still finish, and its result shows)
completed or partially-completed to reverted when Undo succeeds

selectionRules: Only eligible proposed actions can be selected for approval
Blocked actions stay visible but can't be selected
An action that depends on another shows the dependency, and is skipped if that one fails
Approving selected actions never approves unselected ones
Selections survive opening and closing details

reviewSurfaceVariants.inlineCard: For low-risk actions inside an assistant reply or an activity feed
reviewSurfaceVariants.sidePanel: For plans of several actions, where people compare the summary with the details
reviewSurfaceVariants.drawerOrSheet: For phones and tablets, to keep the review connected to the task
reviewSurfaceVariants.modalDialog: For urgent, blocking, high-risk, or irreversible confirmations; it follows the Dialog guide
reviewSurfaceVariants.fullScreen: For long plans, dense diffs, or reviews that need focus

actionTypeGuidance: message: recipients, channel, a preview of the body, attachments, when it sends, and external recipients
record-update: which records, the fields that change, before and after values, and bulk selection
file-operation: the file path, the owner, access changes, where it's shared, and how to revoke it
schedule: attendees, time zone, conflicts, location or conferencing, notes, and external guests
code-change: touched files, the diff, commands, the test plan, permissions, and rollback
payment-or-order: amount, account, recipient, fees, due date, cancellation window, and audit id
external-api: the integration, the operation, the data sent and received, and the permission scope
system-setting: the current and new values, who or what is affected, and whether it can be rolled back

confirmationRules.low: One Approve button, when the affected objects and reversibility are visible
confirmationRules.medium: Show the affected objects and reversibility before approval, and allow editing where parameters matter
confirmationRules.high: An explicit step that states the consequences, with focus on the least destructive action
confirmationRules.irreversible: A typed confirmation that accepts paste (frameworkPatterns.typedConfirmation), or a separate confirmation step that names the consequence. No hold-to-confirm: holding is hard for many people with motor impairments and has no standard keyboard or screen reader behavior.
confirmationRules.blocked: Approval isn't available, and the review says what must change before it can be

implementationDetails.provenance: When a proposal follows content from outside the product, such as an email, a web page, or a shared file, the plan summary says so and links to it: instructions inside such content may not come from the user.
permissionHandling: Show the permission scope in plain language, and why this action needs it
Prefer one-time or task-scoped access to broad, lasting grants
Offer a manual path when permission is denied and the workflow allows it
The server checks the permission and the approval again; hiding or disabling controls is a convenience, not security
Record permission requests and grants as audit events

auditTrail.presentation: A short activity log by default, with technical details behind disclosures.

partialFailureHandling: Keep every action visible after a failure, each with its own state
Retry only failed or skipped actions, and only when it's safe; never rerun a completed action unless the person chooses to

Give each approved action an idempotency key when it's approved and send the same key on every retry (frameworkPatterns.idempotentRetry). Give the request a time limit. Only an answer from the app decides the outcome: no answer, after a timeout or a dropped connection, or an error from a gateway (502 to 504) instead of the app, leaves it unknown, since the action may have run. Say so instead of "Failed", and retry only with the same key, or after checking the status

An answer that only accepts the action, such as 202 Accepted or a pending status in the app's answer, isn't the end: the action stays executing, with its Pause and Stop, and the review tracks it until the app reports how it ended
Before Undo, show what it will revert; if the rollback fails, keep that state and show how to escalate

compositionWithAiPotions.description: This pattern is the control surface of the AI guides. Used with the AI Agent Chat Layout and the AI Response Rendering Pattern, the three divide the work instead of repeating it; each also works alone.
ownedByChatLayout: The shell: the transcript, the composer, and where inline review cards sit in the conversation
ownedByResponseRendering: Tool-call cards and their states (pending, running, success, error, cancelled)
The blocks of the assistant message, its cursor, and its controls
ownedByThisPattern: The review surface: inline card, side panel, drawer, dialog, or full screen
The action model, risk levels, reversibility, and confirmation rules
Approve, reject, edit, revision, pause, stop, retry, and undo
The run's lifecycle, partial failures, the audit trail, and permission requests
coordinationRules: A tool call with consequences, rendered by the AI Response Rendering Pattern, stays pending while this pattern shows it for review, and the reply moves to awaiting-review
Approval moves the action to approved; the tool-call card turns running only when this pattern starts executing it, cancelled on rejection, and error when running it fails
In the AI Agent Chat Layout, low-risk reviews render as cards in the transcript; high-risk or dense plans move to a side panel, drawer, or dialog

Only tool calls the product classifies as without consequences skip review: already authorized, read-only, sending no sensitive data out of the product, and costing nothing meaningful. Reads that send sensitive query data to external services, call metered APIs, or need new permissions are reviewed like any other action

In a conversation, the review's announcements go through the conversation's status region. This pattern renders its own when it runs outside a conversation, and inside the dialog while it's a modal, since the modal hides the conversation's region

desktop.behavior: A side panel, a split view, or full screen for dense plans; the summary and the action list can sit beside the details.

tablet.behavior: The summary above the action list, with dense details behind disclosures.

mobile.behavior: A full-height sheet or a full-screen review, with sticky main controls, safe-area padding, and scroll-padding-bottom equal to the controls' height, so they never cover the focused field, an error, or a status message.

frameworkPatterns.note: Short snippets in plain HTML and JavaScript for the parts that are easiest to get wrong; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

typedConfirmation.description: A typed confirmation for an irreversible action, which accepts paste (implementationDetails.confirmationRules.irreversible).

idempotentRetry.description: Running an approved action with one idempotency key for every attempt. Only the app's answer decides the outcome: 202 Accepted keeps the action executing, and no answer, or a gateway's error, leaves the outcome unknown (implementationDetails.partialFailureHandling).

stateChange.notes: A background or border change when an action's state changes

progress.notes: Progress shows state without constant motion

surfaceEntrance.notes: Follow the project's drawer, sheet, or dialog motion

animations.reducedMotion: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, progress and state changes don't animate, and the status text stays.

framework.description: Find the framework, its version, and how existing components are written before writing code.
detectionSteps: Read the project's dependencies (package.json or its equivalent) for the framework and its version, and use the syntax that version supports.
Open two or three existing components to see their file structure, state handling, and naming.
Look for an existing component that already does this job, in the project or in a design system or UI library it uses, and build on it.

stylingSystem.description: Use the styling system the project already uses, and only that one.
detectionSteps: Check the dependencies and config for the styling setup: Tailwind (version 4 keeps its theme in CSS with @theme, version 3 in tailwind.config.*), CSS Modules, Sass, CSS-in-JS, or plain CSS.
See how existing components apply styles and compose class names, for example with cn or clsx.
Check for design documentation: DESIGN.md, a design system package, or Storybook stories for existing components.
adaptationRules: Write styles the way existing components do, and add no new styling library or system.
With plain CSS, use classes in the project's stylesheets instead of inline styles, except for values computed at runtime.
If the setup is unclear or mixed, ask before choosing.

designTokens.description: Use the project's tokens for color, spacing, radius, type, shadows, motion, and layering.
detectionSteps: Find the tokens: CSS custom properties, a Tailwind theme (@theme or config), a theme object, or a tokens file.
Use them instead of this guide's example values; where there are none, match the closest existing components.
Check that the colors you use meet the contrast minimums: 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for focus indicators, icons, and control boundaries.

must: Build on the project's dialog, drawer, button, checkbox, disclosure, and table components, and its permission and audit services, and keep their APIs
Use the project's framework version, styling system, and tokens, the way existing components do
Implement only the surfaces and controls the task needs
Show proposed actions, and what they affect, before anything runs
Keep partial results in place, and reuse an action's idempotency key on every retry
mustNot: Add a dependency, such as a focus-trap library or a form library, without asking
Run an action from generated prose alone, or approve an unknown action type automatically
Use color alone for risk or status
Treat high-risk and low-risk actions with the same approval
Use inline styles for static values in a plain-CSS project, or hardcode colors the project has tokens for

testingChecklist: Proposed actions show before anything runs, each with what it affects, where it goes, the permission it uses, its risk in text and an icon, and whether it can be undone
Low, medium, high, and blocked actions get the review the confirmation rules give them, and blocked actions can't be approved
Approve is named for the action and its scope, and Approve selected runs only the selected actions
An irreversible action's typed confirmation accepts a pasted phrase, and its button stays focusable and does nothing until the phrase matches
Reject, Edit, and Ask for revision work, and edited values are validated with the project's form rules
Pause and Stop are reachable as soon as actions run, and Stop starts nothing new
After a partial failure, every action shows its own state (completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, or reverted), and Retry runs only failed or skipped actions
An action whose request gets no answer, after a timeout or a dropped connection, says its outcome is unknown, and retrying it reuses its idempotency key, so it never runs twice
An action the app accepts but hasn't finished (202 Accepted) stays executing, with Pause and Stop, until the app reports how it ended
Undo says what it will revert, and its result is recorded
The audit trail records the action, actor, approver, time, tool, permission scope, inputs, outputs, outcome, and rollback
A modal review works like the Dialog guide: focus moves in, the page behind is inert, Escape cancels without approving, and focus returns to the control that opened it
An inline or side-panel review moves focus to its heading when it opens, and progress updates never move focus
Screen readers hear lifecycle changes once each, without the progress log
Sticky controls on phones never cover the focused field, an error, or a status message
With reduced motion, progress and state changes don't animate, and the status text stays
Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, and risk labels, text, and controls meet the contrast minimums

relatedPotions.description: Optional: the AI Agent Chat Layout places review cards in the transcript, or a side panel or dialog, and owns the conversation's status region.
Optional: the AI Response Rendering Pattern renders the tool-call card, which stays pending while this pattern reviews the action, and reflects its result.
Optional: for urgent, blocking, high-risk, or irreversible confirmations.
Optional: for completion, retry, and undo feedback after the review has closed.
Optional: commands with consequences can go through the same review before they run.
Optional: for bulk actions, selectable affected objects, and partial approval.
Optional: for editable action parameters and permission forms.
Optional: keeps risk labels, status colors, and the audit trail readable in both themes.
Optional: for approve, reject, destructive, busy, and icon-only buttons.
